questions.stem: Which of the following best defines marginal costing?
options: A method in which only variable costs are charged to units, and fixed costs are treated as a period cost
A method in which each unit carries a share of fixed production overhead
A method in which only direct materials are charged to units
A method used only for pricing decisions
questions.why: Marginal costing charges variable costs to the product and writes off fixed costs in the period they are incurred.
whyNot: That is absorption costing.
Marginal cost includes direct labour and variable overhead as well as materials.
It is used for a range of short-run decisions, not only pricing.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines absorption costing?
options: A method in which each unit is charged with a share of fixed production overhead as well as its variable costs
A method in which fixed costs are written off in the period incurred
A method in which all overheads, including administration, are charged to units
A method used only for internal decision making
questions.why: The share of fixed production overhead is what distinguishes it, and it is required by IAS 2 for inventory valuation.
whyNot: That is marginal costing.
Only production overhead is absorbed; administration and distribution remain period costs.
Marginal costing is the better method for internal decisions.

questions.stem: Which method must be used to value inventory in published financial statements?
options: Absorption costing
Marginal costing
Either, at the company's choice
Neither: inventory is valued at selling price
questions.why: IAS 2 requires inventory to be valued at full production cost, which means absorption costing.
whyNot: Marginal costing understates inventory for reporting purposes.
The standard does not permit a free choice.
Inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value, not at selling price.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a limiting factor?
options: A resource in short supply that restricts output
The product with the lowest contribution per unit
The maximum price customers will pay
The level of fixed costs a business must cover
questions.why: Machine hours, labour hours or a scarce material can all be limiting factors, and products are then ranked by contribution per unit of that resource.
whyNot: That is a ranking outcome, not the limiting factor itself.
That is a demand constraint on price, not a resource constraint.
Fixed costs affect break-even, not the ranking of products.

questions.stem: Variable production cost is $34 per unit and fixed overhead is absorbed at $15 per unit. What is the absorption cost per unit?
questions.why: Absorption cost = 34 + 15 = $49 per unit.
whyNot: That is the marginal cost, which excludes fixed overhead.
That is the fixed overhead element alone.
That subtracts the two figures.

questions.stem: Fixed production overhead is $150,000 and budgeted output is 10,000 units. What is the absorption rate per unit?
questions.why: 150,000 / 10,000 = $15 per unit. Note the rate is set on budgeted figures, not actual.
whyNot: That uses an incorrect calculation.
That misplaces the decimal point.
That misplaces the decimal point.

questions.stem: Closing inventory is 1,500 units, the variable cost is $34 and the absorption cost is $49. What is the difference in inventory value between the two methods?
questions.why: 1,500 x (49 - 34) = 1,500 x 15 = $22,500 higher under absorption costing.
whyNot: That is the absorption value of the inventory.
That is the marginal value of the inventory.
That is the fixed overhead per unit multiplied by 1,000.

questions.stem: Inventory rose by 1,500 units and fixed overhead is $15 per unit. Which profit is higher and by how much?
options: Absorption profit, by $22,500
Marginal profit, by $22,500
Absorption profit, by $73,500
They are equal
questions.why: Rising inventory means absorption costing carries $22,500 of fixed overhead forward inside the inventory instead of charging it this period.
whyNot: Marginal profit is higher only when inventory falls.
The difference is the change in inventory multiplied by the fixed overhead per unit.
They are equal only when inventory does not change.

questions.stem: Inventory fell during the year. Which profit is higher?
options: Marginal costing profit
Absorption costing profit
They are equal
It depends on the selling price
questions.why: Falling inventory releases fixed overhead brought forward from last period into this period's absorption cost of sales, reducing absorption profit.
whyNot: Absorption profit is higher when inventory rises.
They differ whenever inventory changes.
The selling price affects both methods equally.

questions.stem: Overhead absorbed is $135,000 and overhead incurred is $150,000. What has happened and what is the effect?
options: $15,000 under-absorbed, deducted in the absorption statement
$15,000 over-absorbed, added in the absorption statement
$15,000 under-absorbed, added in the absorption statement
No adjustment is needed
questions.why: Less was charged to production than was incurred, so the shortfall must be deducted from profit.
whyNot: Absorbed is less than incurred, so it is under-absorbed.
Under-absorption is a deduction, not an addition.
The difference must be corrected.

questions.stem: Under-absorption usually arises because:
options: Actual activity fell below the budgeted activity used to set the rate
Actual overhead spending was below budget
The company used marginal costing
Inventory increased during the period
questions.why: The rate is set on budgeted activity, so producing less than budget absorbs less than the overhead incurred.
whyNot: Lower spending, other things equal, would produce over-absorption.
There is no absorption adjustment at all under marginal costing.
Inventory movements affect the profit difference, not absorption.

questions.stem: Normal price $60, variable cost $34, full cost $49. A customer offers $41 per unit for 2,000 units and there is spare capacity. What is the financial effect?
options: Profit rises by $14,000
Profit falls by $16,000
Profit rises by $82,000
Profit is unchanged
questions.why: Contribution = 41 - 34 = $7 per unit, so 2,000 x 7 = $14,000 extra profit, because the fixed costs are being paid anyway.
whyNot: That compares the price with full cost, which is the wrong basis where capacity is spare.
That is total revenue from the order, not the effect on profit.
Any positive contribution changes profit.

questions.stem: Why would an absorption-costing view wrongly reject the order above?
options: The price of $41 is below the full cost of $49, although fixed costs are being paid regardless
Absorption costing ignores variable costs
Absorption costing overstates the contribution
Absorption costing cannot value a special order
questions.why: This is the clearest illustration of why marginal costing is used for short-run decisions.
whyNot: Absorption costing includes variable costs and adds fixed overhead.
It does not calculate contribution at all.
It can value it; the problem is that the valuation misleads the decision.

questions.stem: Which qualitative factor is the strongest argument against accepting a discounted special order?
options: Existing customers may find out and demand the same price
The order will increase total revenue
The order uses spare capacity
The order carries a positive contribution
questions.why: Lost contribution on normal sales could easily exceed the gain on the order, which is why the decision is short run only.
whyNot: Higher revenue is an argument for, not against.
Spare capacity is a condition that supports acceptance.
Positive contribution is the financial case for accepting.

questions.stem: A component costs $18 variable to make, with $40,000 of apportioned fixed overhead of which $12,000 is avoidable. 5,000 are needed and a supplier offers $23. What should be done?
options: Make, saving $13,000
Buy, saving $13,000
Make, saving $25,000
Buy, saving $5,000
questions.why: Cost of making = (5,000 x 18) + 12,000 = $102,000. Cost of buying = 5,000 x 23 = $115,000. Making saves $13,000.
whyNot: Making is cheaper once only the avoidable fixed cost is included.
That omits the $12,000 of avoidable fixed cost from the cost of making.
That uses an incorrect comparison.

questions.stem: Why is the unavoidable $28,000 of fixed overhead excluded from a make-or-buy comparison?
options: It will be incurred either way, so it cannot affect the decision
Fixed overheads are never relevant to any decision
It has already been paid
It belongs to a different department
questions.why: Only relevant costs matter: future cash costs that change as a result of the decision.
whyNot: Avoidable fixed costs are relevant, as the $12,000 shows.
Whether it has been paid is not the test; whether it changes is.
The apportionment is to this product, and it is still unavoidable.

questions.stem: Product C has a contribution of $24,000 and apportioned fixed costs of $44,000, showing a loss of $20,000. Should it be dropped?
options: No, because the $44,000 of fixed costs continues and the $24,000 of contribution would be lost
Yes, because it makes a loss of $20,000
Yes, because its contribution is too low
No, because dropping products is never permitted
questions.why: Dropping C would reduce total profit by $24,000, because the apportioned fixed costs would simply be borne by the other products.
whyNot: The apparent loss is created by the arbitrary apportionment, not by the product.
A positive contribution is worth having when the fixed costs continue.
Products can be dropped; the test is whether contribution is positive and the costs avoidable.

questions.stem: When should a product be discontinued?
options: When its contribution is negative, or its fixed costs are avoidable, or the capacity can earn more elsewhere
Whenever it shows a loss after apportioned fixed costs
Whenever its contribution per unit is the lowest in the range
Whenever its sales revenue is falling
questions.why: Those three conditions are the only sound reasons, and the first is the basic test.
whyNot: An apparent loss after apportionment is not a sound reason.
The lowest contribution may still be positive and worth having.
Falling revenue may still leave a useful contribution.

questions.stem: Contribution per unit: X $36 using 3 hours, Y $28 using 2 hours, Z $45 using 4.5 hours. Which should be made first when machine hours are scarce?
options: Y, at $14.00 per machine hour
Z, because it has the highest contribution per unit
X, at $12.00 per machine hour
All three equally
questions.why: Contribution per machine hour: X $12.00, Y $14.00, Z $10.00. Y ranks first because it earns most from each scarce hour.
whyNot: Z has the highest contribution per unit and the lowest per scarce hour, so it is made last.
X ranks second at $12.00 per hour.
The whole point is that they are not equal per scarce hour.

questions.stem: Why does ranking by contribution per unit give a worse answer when a resource is scarce?
options: A high-contribution product may consume so much of the scarce resource that it earns less per unit of it
Contribution per unit cannot be calculated when a resource is scarce
Fixed costs change when a resource is scarce
Contribution per unit always equals contribution per hour
questions.why: The objective is to maximise contribution from the limited resource, so the resource must be the denominator.
whyNot: It can be calculated; it is simply the wrong ranking basis.
Fixed costs are unaffected by the ranking decision.
They are equal only if every product uses one unit of the resource.

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of marginal costing?
options: Profit is not distorted by inventory movements, which removes the incentive to overproduce
It satisfies IAS 2 for inventory valuation
It ensures prices always cover all costs
It requires no estimate of variable cost
questions.why: Because fixed costs are charged in full each period, building inventory cannot inflate reported profit.
whyNot: Absorption costing is required for published inventory valuation.
Marginal costing risks pricing below full cost, which is one of its weaknesses.
Variable costs must still be estimated.

questions.stem: Which is a disadvantage of absorption costing?
options: The apportionment of fixed overhead is arbitrary and unit cost changes with volume
It cannot be used for published financial statements
It ignores fixed production overhead
It cannot value closing inventory
questions.why: Arbitrary apportionment can make a profitable product look loss-making, and over- and under-absorption complicate the statements.
whyNot: It is required for published statements.
It includes fixed production overhead, which is its defining feature.
It values inventory at full production cost.

questions.stem: Why can a manager judged on absorption profit have an incentive to overproduce?
options: Building inventory carries fixed overhead forward and raises reported profit
Overproduction reduces variable cost per unit
Overproduction reduces total fixed costs
Absorption costing ignores unsold units
questions.why: Marginal costing removes this incentive, which is one of the strongest arguments for using it internally.
whyNot: Variable cost per unit is unchanged by volume in this model.
Total fixed costs do not fall with higher output.
Unsold units are exactly what carries the overhead forward.
